hints: Focus on what it means when one compound turns into another with no other products formed.
Start with what you know for sure, the ammonium ion is $\text{NH}_4^+$ and urea is $\text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2$.
Count atoms and charges to work out what the second ion must supply to make the totals match urea exactly.
walkthrough:
**Spot that atoms are conserved**

This is an isomerisation. Ammonium cyanate changes into urea only, so both solids must contain exactly the same atoms in total.

$$\text{ammonium cyanate} \rightarrow \text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2$$

**Write out what urea contains**

Urea looks complicated, but just count it. $\text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2$ contains 1 C, 1 O, 2 N and 4 H.

$$\text{urea} = \text{C}_1\text{H}_4\text{N}_2\text{O}_1$$

**Subtract the ammonium ion**

Ammonium cyanate is $\text{NH}_4^+$ plus the cyanate ion. The $\text{NH}_4^+$ already supplies 1 N and 4 H.

So the cyanate ion must supply what is left: 1 C, 1 O and 1 N.
$$\text{C}_1\text{H}_4\text{N}_2\text{O}_1 - \text{N}_1\text{H}_4 = \text{C}_1\text{O}_1\text{N}_1$$

**Balance the charge**

The solid is neutral and $\text{NH}_4^+$ is 1+, so the cyanate ion must be 1- to cancel it.

That gives $\text{OCN}^-$, with one of each atom and a single negative charge.

options.A: Incorrect. This suggests $\text{CON}_2^-$ with two N atoms. Added to $\text{NH}_4^+$, that would give 3 N atoms in total, but urea only has 2 N atoms. It also writes C before O, which is not the accepted order for cyanate.
options.B: Incorrect. This suggests $\text{CON}_2^{2-}$ with two N atoms and a 2- charge. That gives too many N atoms and the charges would not balance: $\text{NH}_4^+$ plus 2- would leave an overall 1- charge, not neutral.
options.C: Correct. $\text{OCN}^-$ has 1 O, 1 C and 1 N with a 1- charge. Together with $\text{NH}_4^+$, the total is $\text{C}_1\text{H}_4\text{N}_2\text{O}_1$ with zero overall charge, exactly matching urea, $\text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2$.
options.D: Incorrect. This has the right atoms, O, C and N, but the wrong charge of 2-. A 2- anion cannot form a neutral salt with a single $\text{NH}_4^+$ ion, it would need two ammonium ions and that would double the H and N count.
